This certainly can be handled correctly in NIMBLE, although depending on exactly how you're using your custom-written distribution (for MCMC?), it might require a small amount of care in getting the implementation correct.

A good start will be supplying the "range" argument when you call registerDistributions, with the correct lower and upper bounds.

It would also be good to make sure your custom-written density function returns -Inf (when returning the log-density), when the random variable falls outside te support.

It will sometimes give some warning messages if you do pure R execution (e.g. using the uncompiled model object, or running an uncompiled MCMC).  But these warnings won't show up when you're using the compiled versions of the model and MCMC.

Hope this helps!

> My question is: is there any advantage in NIMBLE in vectorising user-defined distribution functions? Currently all my applications are MCMC.

One advantage is to reduce the number of nodes used to represent the model - this can translate to reducing the CPU time spend to get a model running. e.g. for a time-series, instead of having one node per time step, you might define a vectorised distribution that works with the entire time series (just one node).  In this scenario I would consider vectorising if the CPU time for getting the model running was an issue.

messages.body_plain:
To generalize upon David's response: a good way to think about when to vectorize is how having a single vector node vs. many scalar nodes impacts the graph that represents your model.  When an MCMC sampler operates on a node or nodes (the "target"), it must calculate the nodes that depend on the target node(s).   If the part of the model you might vectorize will always need to be calculated together anyway, then vectorizing makes sense.  On the other hand, if one element of what you might vectorize corresponds to one stochastic node updated by one sampler, then it may be better to stay with scalar nodes, so that a sampler for one of the stochastic nodes is not burdened with calculations over the whole vector that are not really necessary.  Does that make sense?

In general, we tend to see much greater gains in MCMC efficiency from customizing the sampling scheme than from re-writing (e.g. vectorizing) the model, but sometimes the latter does indeed help a lot.

A major difference from Stan is that, if I understand correctly, Stan always calculates the entire model, so vectorization where possible is always helpful.  It does not create a graph and then calculate only portions of the model that are needed for particular samplers (as NIMBLE does), because it samples all model states jointly.  While HMC is great, customized sampler configurations in NIMBLE can sometimes be more efficient than Stan.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jeremey,

You can't use conditionals like that in the model.  if-then-else is not part of the BUGS language.

The reason is that this is a declarative language.  Every declaration creates one or more nodes in a graphical model.  From that perspective, one can't have a graph with conditional relationships.  In your example it would be conceptually simple since x depends on nu in both conditional outcomes, but the difficulty would be a case where different conditional outcomes lead to different dependencies among nodes.

NIMBLE does support if-then-else statements that will be evaluated *once, at the time of model definition* (i.e. when calling nimbleModel).  That means that when you call nimbleModel, the conditionals are evaluated, and only one of the outcomes is built into the model.  The purpose of that is to allow alternative models to be defined from the same code.

You can accomplish what you want to do by writing a nimbleFunction for the way you want xi to depend on nu.  You would use:

xi <- myFun(nu) ## in the model code

and, in R:

myFun <- nimbleFunction(
run = function(nu = double(0)) {
> if(nu < 2){
>     ans <- log(nu)
>   }
>   else
>     ans <- nu / 2
>  }
  return(ans)
  returnType(double(0))
})

By doing it this way, the graph of the model can be built using the declaration that xi depends on nu, via myFun(nu).  Within myFun, the code is familiar imperative programming, so you can use conditionals as needed.

If there was a case where in one conditional outcome x is calculated from nu and in another outcome x is calculated from eta (say), then one would use "x <- myFun(nu, eta)".  From the graph perspective, x would always depend on both nu and eta, regardless of how the actual calculation (with whatever conditionals may be involved) turns out.

Let me know if any of that does not make sense.

I am getting a fatal error when my model with my user-defined distribution is compiling with nimbleMCMC. The error message is:
> >  Error: In sizeAssignAfterRecursing: 'return' is not available or its output type is unknown.
> >  This occurred for: Interm_21 <- return(-((pow(z1,(-(inv_xi))))) - log(ARG3_sigma_))
> >  This was part of the call:

Nothing follows the final colon.

My user-defined distribution is intended to be the generalised extreme value distribution. It is slightly complicated because the support of the distribution depends on the shape parameter, xi, so that if xi < 0, the support is bounded above, if xi > 0, it is bounded below, and if xi = 0 it is unbounded.

Here is my function:
> >
> > dnimgev <- nimbleFunction(
> >   run = function(x = double(0),
> >                  mu = double(0),
> >                  sigma = double(0),
> >                  xi = double(0),
> >                  log = integer(0, default = 0)) {
> >     returnType(double(0))
> >
> >     if (abs(xi) > 1e-15){
> >       inv_xi <- 1 / xi
> >       # Weibull and Frechet cases
> >       # Weibull: xi < 0, x bounded above by mu - sigma / xi
> >       # Frechet: xi <0, x bounded below by mu - sigma / xi
> >       z1 <- 1 + (x - mu) * xi / sigma
> >       # z1 < 0 implies density = 0 in both cases
> >
> >       if (z1 > 0)
> >         if (log == 1)
> >           return(-(z1 ^ (-inv_xi)) - log(sigma)) - (1 + inv_xi) * log(z1)
> >         else
> >           return(exp(-(z1 ^ (-inv_xi))) * (1 / sigma) * z1 ^ -(1 + inv_xi))
> >
> >       else
> >         if (log == 1)
> >           return(-Inf)
> >         else
> >         return(0)
> >
> >     }
> >     else{
> >       # Gumbel case: unbounded support
> >       z1 <- (x - mu) / sigma
> >       if(log == 1)
> >         return(- exp(- z1) - log(sigma) - z1)
> >       else
> >         return(exp(- exp(- z1)) * (1 / sigma) * exp(-(z1)))
> >     }
> >   })
>

Any help would be appreciated. I am wondering whether the compiler is worried that sigma might be negative or xi , so that log(sigma) would fail. In fact sigma is constrained in the model to be strictly positive. Maybe the compiler does not know this? I have tried writing an explicit constraint sigma > 0 into the model but that makes no difference to the fatal error.

Another thought is that if xi = 0, then inv_xi = Inf, but inv_xi is only defined for the cases where xi \neq 0.

An earlier version  of this function did run,  did not require  a random generation function, and produced sensible-looking results. (I had made a mistake in the formula for the distribution. That was why I moved on to this new version.) The first time I tried to run this version, however,  I got
>  Error in eval(as.name <http://as.name>(simulateName)) : object 'rnimgev' not found

So I wrote a  random generation function. I found it odd that it was required in one case and not the other.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Seongjeun,

Thanks for the question.

It looks like with PREDICT_Y == TRUE, there is no mixing at all in the model.  I may not be following everything, but it looks like this occurs because Inits$z_sigma is 0, which means all zy_p[i] values are 0 and have logProb_zy_p[i] of Inf, and all logProb_zy[i] are -Inf.  The sampling is never able to get away from this state.

When PREDICT_Y == FALSE, the initial states still have z_sigma == 0 and all logProb_zy[i] are -Inf.  However, any non-zero value of z_sigma in the first MCMC iteration would be accepted because it would raise the logProb_zy[i] to real values and hence be an infinite improvement.  When PREDICT_Y == TRUE, I think this would be defeated by the logProb_zy_p[i] values of Inf, which would make any change in z_sigma give infinitely worse fit.

In any case, can you try initializing z_sigma with a value > 0?

It still may not be a good idea to include stochastic posterior predictive nodes, because they will slow your mixing.  One strategy for posterior prediction is to make another nimbleModel for that purpose.  You would then iterate over the posterior sample from the first model, put each set of states into the posterior prediction model, and use it for simulation as needed.  Of course in a simple case like yours, you could also do it more directly.  If you use the mvSamples directly, you can access variables in it by name.

Perry

While I'm not sure about this particular case, I can say there are cases where NIMBLE benefits more (i.e. is more sensitive) from useful initial values than does JAGS.  To some extent, this has to do with which samplers are used.

messages.body_plain:
Hello there, I am a PhD student using nimble to develop hidden Markov and hidden semi-Markov rainfall models.

This is a simplest version I can come up with of the problem I am having with the compiler. Suppose I have a vector of n values from a mixture distribution of a Bernoulli(1-p) and some positive distribution e.g. Exponential(theta):

0 , 1.54439307 , 0.12542128 , 0 , 0.52887174 , 0.98874485 , 0 , 0.02455954 , 0 , 0 , ...

The probability densities for these values are given by:

p(x|theta,p)=          p if x=0
                              (1-p)*dexp(x,theta) if x>0

This is straightforward to implement in nimble using a nimbleFunction with if statements and a for loop over the vector of x values. However, in R this can instead be written as:

dens = p*(x==0) + (1-p)*dexp(x,theta)*(x>0)

However, the compiler doesn't seem to manage this version (failed to create the shared library). If the vector of values is very long then the for loop is much slower. In my particular case, it takes 4-5 seconds to evaluate the non-compiled function with a loop in R, compared to 2-3 seconds if it is written as above. I've tried to solve this several times over a last few months, as my knowledge of nimble improves, but I haven't found a solution yet. Here's some code if anyone is interested in trying to reproduce my problem. If anyone is able to get this model to work without using a loop then it would go some way to helping me solve my own problem, for which I would be very grateful!

Thank you!

p <- 0.8
theta <- 1
N <- 1000
x <- rexp(N,theta)*rbinom(N,1,1-p)

dziexp <- nimbleFunction(run=function(x=double(1),p=double(0),theta=double(0),N=double(0),log=integer(0)){
  returnType(double(0))
  return(sum(log(p*(x==0) + (1-p)*dexp(x,theta)*(x>0))))
})

rziexp <- nimbleFunction(run=function(n=integer(0),p=double(0),theta=double(0),N=double(0)){
  returnType(double(1))
  return(rexp(N,1)*rbinom(N,1,1-p))
})

registerDistributions(list(
  dziexp = list(
    BUGSdist = 'dziexp(p,theta,N)',
    types = c('value=double(1)','p=double(0)','theta=double(0)','N=double(0)'),
    mixedSizes = TRUE
  )
))

ziCode <- nimbleCode({
  x[1:n]~dziexp(p,theta,n)
  p~dunif(0,1)
  theta~dunif(0,10)
})

ziConsts <- list(n=N)
ziData <- list(x=x)
ziInits <- list(p=0.5,theta=1)

ziModel <- nimbleModel(ziCode, ziConsts,ziData,ziInits)
ziCModel <- compileNimble(ziModel,resetFunctions = TRUE)

zimcmcConf <- configureMCMC(ziModel,monitors=c('theta','p'),useConjugacy = FALSE)
zimcmcConf$removeSamplers('theta')
zimcmcConf$addSampler('theta',type='slice')

zimcmc<-buildMCMC(zimcmcConf)
ziCmcmc<-compileNimble(zimcmc, project = ziModel,resetFunctions = TRUE)
ziSamples<-runMCMC(ziCmcmc,
                      nchains = 2, nburnin=500,niter = 1000,samplesAsCodaMCMC = TRUE,
                      summary = FALSE, WAIC = FALSE)
plot(ziSamples)

    }
})

INDS <- c(1, 3, 5) ## indices where bool_vec is TRUE

m <- nimbleModel(mc, constants = list(INDS = INDS, INDS2 = INDS2))

Improving compile time is one of our long-term development goals.  Unfortunately I can't give any great tricks.  You can speed up nimbleModel by using calculate = FALSE, check = FALSE.  You can speed up configureMCMC by using useConjugacy = FALSE if you do not actually need any Gibbs samplers.  But there's not much we can do for the compiler until we manage some real development advances.

Perry

We’ve released the newest version of NIMBLE on CRAN and on our website.

Version 0.6-11 has important new features, notably support for
Bayesian nonparametric mixture modeling, and more are on the way in
the next few months.

New features include:

 - support for Bayesian nonparametric mixture modeling using Dirichlet
process mixtures, with specialized MCMC samplers automatically
assigned in NIMBLE’s default MCMC (See Chapter 10 of the manual for
details);
 - additional resampling methods available with the auxiliary and
bootstrap particle filters;
user-defined filtering algorithms can be used with NIMBLE’s particle
MCMC samplers;
 - MCMC thinning intervals can be modified at MCMC run-time;
 - both runMCMC() and nimbleMCMC() now drop burn-in samples before
thinning, making their behavior consistent with each other;
 - increased functionality for the ‘setSeed’ argument in nimbleMCMC()
and runMCMC();
 - new functionality for specifying the order in which sampler
functions are executed in an MCMC; and
 - invalid dynamic indexes now result in a warning and NaN values but
do not cause execution to error out, allowing MCMC sampling to
continue.

Please see the NEWS file in the installed package for more details.

- Chris Paciorek for the NIMBLE Development Team

messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

This is a probably a really simple query but one that I seem to be having difficulty with.  I have written a custom distribution for NIMBLE that takes a vector is one of its arguments.  It is often used in the model specification in a similar way to this:

nimbleCode({
   # Prior on the scalar parameter
   myScalarParameter ~ dnorm(0.0, 0.001)
   # Use the parameter and a covariate to make an input argument for the distribution
   myInputArgument[1:numData] <- myScalarParameter * myCovariate[1:numData]
   # Likelihood calculation
   myData[1:numData] ~ dMyCustomDistribution(myInputArgument[1:numData])
})

However, in some cases, it will be more natural to provide a scalar argument here because, in many of our applications, this argument will not vary.  It would be nice to be able to write something like the following in the model specification:

nimbleCode({
    # Prior on the scalar parameter
    myScalarParameter ~ dnorm(0.0, 0.001)
    # Likelihood calculation
    myData[1:numData] ~ dMyCustomDistribution(myScalarParameter)
})

When I do this NIMBLE obviously complains that myScalarParameter is not a vector (which it isn't).  So, simple question: what is the best way to promote myScalarParameter to a 1-length vector (my custom function recycles the input vector to get an input vector of the right length)?

I've tried the following solutions but none of these seem to work:

nimbleCode({
   myScalarParameter[1] ~ dnorm(0.0, 0.001)
   myData[1:numData] ~ dMyCustomDistribution(myScalarParameter)
})
nimbleCode({
   myScalarParameter ~ dnorm(0.0, 0.001)
   myData[1:numData] ~ dMyCustomDistribution(c(myScalarParameter))
})

This seems to work but seems... clunky.

nimbleCode({
   # Prior on the scalar parameter
   myScalarParameter ~ dnorm(0.0, 0.001)
   # Make a vectorised version of the parameter
   for(dataIter in 1:numData) {
      myVectorisedParameter[dataIter] <- myScalarParameter
   }
   # Likelihood calculation
   myData[1:numData] ~ dMyCustomDistribution(myVectorisedParameter[1:numData])
})

I could of course make another custom distribution for the use of scalar arguments but that also would result in lots of annoying code replication and seems inelegant.

I'm just wondering if I'm missing something obvious.  I can provide the specific code for my case if that helps but I think my question here is more conceptual than implementation-specific.

Thank you in advance for any help you can provide.

All the best,

Joe

   run = function(inputArg = double() {

       inputArgVec <- numeric(value = inputArg, length = myLength, recycle = TRUE)
       # Run the vectorised version of the function
       return(dmyDistribution_Vector(inputArgVec))
   }
)

Joe

Hi Joe,

Thanks for this question.

Unfortunately, there are a variety of corners where nimble's hard typing creates limitations, and this is one of them.  It's something we hope to improve in a deeper renovation, although maybe we should try to do something superficial faster.

One possible workaround would be to always make the argument to dMyCustomDistribution be a vector by padding it with a dummy value if necessary.  E.g.

myParameter[1] <- whatever_you_really_need
myParameter[2] <- 0 ## a dummy to make myParameter a true vector.

Then when you call dMyCustomDistribution, you could include an additional argument indicating whether myParameter is padded in this way.

Oh no, I just noticed that in the newly released nimble 0.6-12, there is a bug in the automatic creation of "r" functions for custom distributions (when the user doesn't provide the "r" function).  We added a new error trap for missing return() statements, and the dummy version of the "r" function now errors out for this reason.  Evidently we don't have that case in our test suite.  I'll go post an issue on github.

Perry

nimbleCode({
   # Prior on the scalar parameter

   myScalarParameter[1] ~ dnorm(0.0, 0.001)
   # This only need to be length 2 as it just needs to be greater than one to trick NIMBLE into accepting
   # these arguments as a vector
   myScalarParameter[2] <- myScalarParameter[1]
   # Likelihood calculation (myScalarParameter gets recycled to the desired length internally in the distribution)
   myData[1:numData] ~ dMyCustomDistribution(myScalarParameter[1:2])
})

I can imagine changing the underlying structure of NIMBLE to interpret scalars as 1-length vectors for functions that only accept vector input may cause a lot of headaches and may not even be desirable behaviour in many cases but a function/macro-like-thing that allows for the user to force this interpretation in particular cases (to allow for something like 'distributionWithVectorArg(Promote_To_Vector(aScalarVariable))') without having to create extra logical nodes would be super useful I think.

Dear Matt,

Thanks for the question.  I can't reproduce your example without your data file (nrow(LagTemp) is the first hurdle), but I think I see the issue.

Especially in model code, nimble's hard typing can be confusing when one is used to dynamic type conversions in R.  In this case, matrix multiplication returns a matrix (as it does in R), and dl.effect[d,a] is a scalar (it is a length-1 vector in R).  In R, the assignment from a 1x1 matrix into a non-matrix is automatically converted due to *run-time* checking of the matrix size.  In nimble, all types are determined at compile time (as in C++), so you need to tell nimble that you know the matrix will be in effect a scalar.  A way to do so would be:

 dl.effect[d,a] <- (Temps[d,1:(L+1)]%*%(DLBasis[((a-1)*(L+1)+1):((a-1)*(L+1)+1+L),1:n.DLBasis]%*%beta.DL[1:n.DLBasis]))[1,1]

The previous question on the list was also about the friction of scalar <--> non-scalar conversions.  It's something we hope to make smoother in future renovations, although maybe we should try to put together shorter-term accommodations.

Perry

messages.body_plain:
There isn't a way to use the model with multiple sets of variables in one go.  Instead what you need to do is iterate over the sample, put one set of values into the model, simulate or calculate whatever you need, and copy the results out of the model.  There are two strategies for iterating over a sample.  You can keep the sample in its modelValues object (the way it is stored from the MCMC) and use nimCopy to put values in the model.  Or you can keep it as a matrix and use values(model, nodes) <- some_values to put values in the model. I can send an example soon but not at this moment.
-Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hello all,
I am a quantitative ecologist - i.e. not a programmer or a statistician - and I use JAGS through R quite a bit to run hierarchical Bayesian models. I am trying to use nimble in the same way I use JAGS in an attempt to speed things up on models that take a long time in JAGS (like 3 weeks) and use a great deal of memory for the processing and output.

My questions are:
1. Can I use parallel processing with nimble, i.e. send individual MCMC chains to separate cores (and if so, how? - I can't find anything on the internet about this)? I've tried with doParallel and can't get it to work.

2. Is there any way to update the models after they have finished if the haven't converged yet?

Thank you in advance for any help you can give or resources you can point me to.

Andrew D. Crosby
Postdoctoral Fellow
Boreal Avian Modelling Project
Dept. of Biological Sciences
CW405 Biological Sciences Building
University of Alberta
Edmonton, AB T6G 2E9

messages.body_plain:
I can give an easy answer to #2:

>> Is there any way to update the models after they have finished if the haven't converged yet?

If you use the lowest-level entry point to NIMBLE's MCMC engine, the run() method of the compiled MCMC object, then at that level there's the ability to "continue" an on-going run using reset=FALSE.  Note the different syntax for extracting the posterior samples after using this method.

Rmodel <- nimbleModel(code, constants, data, inits)

conf <- configureMCMC(Rmodel)
Rmcmc <- buildMCMC(conf)
Cmodel <- compileNimble(Rmodel)
Cmcmc <- compileNimble(Rmcmc, project = Rmodel)

Cmcmc$run(10000)
samples <- as.matrix(Cmcmc$mvSamples)

## examine samples array, determine it hasn't converged yet...

## continue that same run of the MCMC for 50000 more iterations:
Cmcmc$run(50000, reset = FALSE)

samplesAll60000 <- as.matrix(Cmcmc$mvSamples)

Let me know if this answers your question.

Cheers,
Daniel
